facts.value: Capital and Investment Strategy Outturn 2025/26 to Governance Scrutiny Group, Thursday 18 June 2026. Report of the Director – Finance and Corporate Services (Peter Linfield). 15 pages including a one-page glossary appendix. Covers Treasury Management (paras 4.1-4.26) and the Asset Investment Strategy (paras 4.27-4.39). Contact block page 14: Peter Linfield, 0115 914 8439, plinfield@rushcliffe.gov.uk. Read in full from local PDF on 2026-08-16.

source.title: Capital and Investment Strategy Outturn 2025/26 – Governance Scrutiny Group, 18 June 2026

facts.note: This outturn is a complete stand-alone report — Table 1 through Table 12 all in-body; no separate appendix required. Background papers list references Statement of Accounts 2025/26; Capital and Investment Strategy 2025/26; Treasury Management Update – Mid-Year Report 2025/26 and quarters 1 to 3 reports 2025/26 — none held. Paper does not name the Section 151 Officer separately from Peter Linfield's role as Director – Finance and Corporate Services; on constitutional convention that role would typically hold the S151 title, but this must be verified separately from the paper alone before addressing as S151.

facts.value: TIES ZERO ON ZERO. python3 monitor/outreach/price_book.py --find "Rushcliffe" returns 'no borrower matching Rushcliffe' (only RUSHMOOR BOROUGH COUNCIL is a name-adjacent match, verified as a different Hampshire council). Paper para 4.14 (page 4) states: 'the Council had no recourse to borrow externally during 2025/26 these indicators are not applicable.' Prudential-limit context: Authorised Limit for external debt was £20m and Operational Boundary £15m — both precautionary; neither approached. Zero in our file, zero in the paper — the two agree.

source.title: OUR file — price_book.py --find and --as-at; paper para 4.14 and paras 4.13-4.15 (page 4)

facts.note: Same shape as Rochford (E07000075) — the strongest form the loan-book cross-check can take for a debt-free council. Safe to open the email with.

facts.value: PARTIALLY CHECKED. CFR £8.417m at 31 March 2026 (Table 3, page 3) less external borrowing £0 (para 4.14) less other long-term liabilities — the OLTL balance is NOT PRINTED anywhere in the paper. Only the movement is disclosed: +£2.773m in 2024/25 for initial IFRS 16 recognition, +£66k in 2025/26 as recalculation. Total lease liability at 31.3.26 not derivable from this paper alone. Sanity check on internal position: NHB Reserve balance is £8.383m at page 9 and the paper describes it explicitly as funding 'internal borrowing for Capital projects (MRP Minimum Revenue Provision)' — £8.383m sits very close to the £8.417m CFR, consistent with the reserve underwriting essentially the whole internal position. Para 4.11 also states 'No internal borrowing was needed in 2025/26' which we read as 'no additional internal borrowing was drawn during the year' rather than 'internal borrowing is zero' — the reserve arithmetic supports that reading.

source.title: Table 3 (page 3), para 4.11, para 4.14, Table 10 balance sheet resources (page 9)

facts.note: The identity cannot be closed exactly because the OLTL total is not printed. Not a criticism of the paper — the CFR movement (10,010 + 66 - 1,659 = 8,417) ties to the pound and the reserve position is stated with clarity. But means the internal borrowing figure is not a fact we can quote in the email. Recorded here as a coverage gap on our side of the reading.

facts.value: CFR at 31 March 2026 £8.417m closing (£10.010m opening + £66k IFRS 16 adjustment - £1.659m MRP; ties). Capital expenditure 2025/26 £10.862m against a revised budget of £14.873m — 73% delivery, £4.011m under. £3.145m carry-forward requested for Cabinet approval in July 2026. Increase in borrowing need = £0 across all three years shown in Table 2 (2024/25 actual, 2025/26 estimate and actual). Arena scheme MRP will be repaid in full in 2026-27, at which point MRP will reduce and VRP (which only applies to the Arena) will stop.
facts.note: The Arena is a specific council-owned asset with a bespoke MRP arrangement (£0.250m MRP over 40 years plus £0.750m VRP) funded from NHB Reserve. The Arena being paid off in 2026-27 is a specific event that will bring the total MRP charge down materially in 2027-28 onwards. Not a hook in itself but relevant context — the NHB Reserve (£8.383m) is 'sufficient to cover MRP payments for the remainder of the MTFS' after Arena roll-off.

facts.value: Total investments £72.598m at 31 March 2026 (para 4.19 Table 7 and Table 8 total row £72,597,656). Weighted average interest rate 4.33% for 2025/26 (para 4.21) — 27bp above the 4.06% budget and 32bp above the SONIA average of 4.01%. Net return £2,051,880 vs budget £1,434,900 = +£616,980 favourable. Composition of the book at 31.3.26: pooled funds £14.251m (5 funds); money market funds £19.183m (8 MMFs); LA fixed-term deposits £25.000m (5 councils); Standard Chartered secured £6.000m; unsecured bank residuals ~£8.164m across HSBC/BoS/Barclays/Handelsbanken/Santander. No sums invested over one year (Table 7). Bank Rate ended 2025/26 at 3.75% (para 4.20 — dropped to 3.75% in December 2025 'where it remains today').
facts.note: Large investment book relative to CFR (£72.6m vs £8.4m). Rushcliffe is a substantial net investor and the outturn ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream is NEGATIVE at (1.33%) — Table 4, page 5 — because investment income exceeded MRP. The 4.33% outturn rate beat the budget by 27bp on a £72.6m book, which is the £617k. Distinctive characteristic: 5 LA counterparties at exactly £5m each — clear concentration cap.

facts.value: One of Rushcliffe's five LA fixed-term deposits at 31.3.26 stands out. Havant Borough Council took £5.000m from Rushcliffe at 5.60% for 30 days, maturing 17/04/2026 (Table 8, page 7). The other four LA deposits sit at 4.25%–4.30% for tenors of 181-364 days (Cheshire East 4.30% 364d, Blackpool 4.25% 181d, Leeds 4.25% 212d, Lancashire 4.25% 364d). The 5.60% rate is ~160bp over SONIA (4.01% para 4.21) and 185bp over Bank Rate (3.75% at time of drawdown ~mid-March 2026) for 30-day money — a stand-out rate for the tenor. We hold Havant's own Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 in the library (E07000090.json): Havant runs a very small external book (one PWLB loan of £2.7m, maturing 2042) against a £22m CFR — 88% internally funded. A 30-day LA-to-LA bridge at 5.60% fits the profile of an internally-funded district needing a short cash top-up without drawing PWLB.

source.title: Rushcliffe Table 8 (page 7); paras 4.20 and 4.21 (page 7). Cross-checked against Havant TMS 2026/27 in E07000090.json.

facts.note: This is the strongest single hook in the paper for us. Rushcliffe caught the receive side of an unusual short-tenor LA-to-LA trade — the platform sees the borrower side of that market via its other treasury readings. Havant's own paper is a strategy not an outturn so it does not explicitly narrate the March 2026 short cash need — but the profile is entirely consistent. In the email, name the shape (a stand-out short-tenor rate on a small deposit) without asserting Havant's motive from our side — that is theirs to explain if they want to.

facts.value: £15.000m invested across five diversified pooled funds; fair value at 31.3.26 £14.251m; cumulative unrealised deficit £749,173 vs initial investment (Table 9, page 8). During 2025/26 the fair value INCREASED by £321,957 — the £749k is the residual from earlier mark-to-market losses partially unwinding. Aegon (Kames) at £5.0m invested is at £4.937m (-£63k on initial); Ninety One (Investec) at £5.0m is at £4.566m (-£434k); CCLA Cautious at £2.0m is at £1.721m (-£279k) — three funds account for essentially the whole deficit. RLAM and CCLA Property are slightly above the invested amount. Council holds a £1.310m reserve to mitigate any losses (para 4.22). Statutory override effective to April 2029 currently prevents any accounting loss impacting the General Fund (para 4.22). Diversified funds returned 4.70% average in 2025/26, above both MMFs and Base Rate (para 4.23).
facts.note: The statutory override runs to April 2029 — a widely-shared position across councils holding pooled funds. Rushcliffe's approach of holding a bespoke £1.310m reserve alongside the override is worth noting. £1.310m against £749k current deficit is ~1.75x cover for the current mark-to-market position. Not a distress signal — the fair value moved in the council's favour during 2025/26. Worth noting in the email as the shape of a defensively-provisioned position.

facts.value: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream came in NEGATIVE at (1.33%) for 2025/26 actual, against a POSITIVE 1.67% budgeted (Table 4, page 5). Prior year 2024/25 was (4.95%) actual. The paper is explicit: 'The actual is negative figure as a result of higher income from investments due to interest rates throughout the year remaining above expectations, resulting in income exceeding MRP payments.' Net financing costs 2025/26 actual: (£276k) — investment income exceeded the £1.659m MRP charge by ~£276k. Net Income from commercial and service investments (Table 5, page 5) 2025/26 actual £2.251m against budget £2.097m and prior year £1.905m; ratio to net revenue stream 10.9%.
facts.note: The negative financing costs ratio is a distinctive prudential-indicator marker of the debt-free-plus-cash-rich shape — same pattern as Rochford (E07000075 at -6.76%) though at a much less negative level because Rushcliffe carries a £1.659m MRP charge each year against Rochford's essentially nil MRP. The two ratios in combination (financing costs -1.33% and commercial contribution 10.9%) tell the full story: MRP is more than covered by treasury income, and commercial income sits on top.

facts.value: Table 6 (page 5) shows Fixed Interest Rate exposure at 43% actual against a 50% limit; Variable exposure at 57% against a 100% limit (i.e. no restriction). Para 4.18 (page 5): 'The Strategy states that whilst the Council has set a limit of 50% on fixed interest rate exposure, during a time of falling interest rates, as the UK was experiencing during 2025/26, the indicator should not be restrictive preventing the Council from locking into higher interest rates.' The Council sat below its own fixed-rate limit at year-end — i.e. it did not exercise the flexibility the strategy carved out to lock into higher fixed rates ahead of the December 2025 cut. Base Rate held at 3.75% from December 2025 through today (para 4.20 written mid-June 2026; still 3.75% at 2026-08-16).
facts.note: Interesting stated-strategy-vs-outturn pattern. The strategy was written to allow locking into fixed at higher rates in anticipation of the cutting cycle; the outturn shows 57% variable at year-end. If rates cut further from 3.75%, the variable book takes an immediate yield hit. If rates hold or rise, the variable book benefits. Not a criticism — the £5m/364-day LA deposits at 4.25-4.30% ARE the fixed side. But the shape is notable.

facts.value: AIS portfolio £16.137m across nine commercial property investments plus the NCCC (Notts County Cricket Club) loan (Table 11, page 10). Gross return column shows 3.05%-7.83% across sites; the paper prints a Total 6.02% but on our arithmetic 949,267 / 16,137,154 = 5.88%. The 14bp gap is a presentational quirk in the paper (Cotgrave Industrial Units line £137,957 sits under Cotgrave Offices without its own Investment Value; may account for the discrepancy). Table 12 (page 13) shows commercial property income £1.920m actual vs £1.979m budget (-£59k), running costs £518k actual vs £473k budget (+£45k), net contribution to core functions £1.402m against £1.506m budget. Total contribution including commercial loan interest £1.462m. Total contribution/total income ratio 9.8% actual vs 12.5% budget — total income grew faster than commercial contribution.
facts.note: Para 4.28: 'The Council no longer invests in property for commercial gain.' Para 4.34: 'Revised PWLB borrowing rules have been introduced to ensure that no lending they issue is used primarily for commercial investment. While the Council has no plans to borrow during the MTFS the Council remains compliant with these rules. Going forward, investment income as a result of the AIS will only increase with rent increases rather than in growth of the portfolio from acquisitions.' Portfolio is closed to further acquisition — a policy position triggered by the 2020 PWLB lending rules revision. Not a hook per se but relevant context. Would prefer not to raise in a first-contact email — commercial-property questions from us to an S151-adjacent role read as more probing than we mean them to be.

facts.value: Balance Sheet Resources at 31.3.26 (Table 10, page 9): General Fund Balance £2.604m (unchanged year-on-year); Earmarked Reserves £28.664m (up from £24.287m — net transfer to earmarked £4.375m); Usable Capital Receipts £2.386m (down from £5.762m — used to fund capital programme); Capital Grants Unapplied £73k. Total £33.727m against prior year £32.795m. Named reserves: NHB Reserve £8.383m (funds internal borrowing / MRP); Organisation Stabilisation Reserve £8.121m; LGR Reserve £1.199m (set aside for Local Government Reorganisation implementation costs including training and additional staff).
facts.note: LGR reserve £1.199m confirms Rushcliffe is preparing for Nottinghamshire local government reorganisation. Do not raise this in the email — the political sensitivity of LGR is high and it's not treasury-relevant to a first-contact reading. Recorded for library context: Rushcliffe as a legal entity may not exist to receive follow-up in 18-24 months.

facts.value: Missing from this paper: no total OLTL/lease-liability balance at 31.3.26 (only the year-on-year movement of +£66k is stated in Table 3); no maturity structure of the investment book beyond the individual-deposit maturity dates in Table 8 and the 'sums invested over one year = £0' line in Table 7; no principal-weighted split between fixed and variable segments (Table 6 only prints the % ratios); no adviser named anywhere in the paper; no explicit forward-year projections of investment income or portfolio composition; no LB chart data table (only the graphical Chart 1). These absences are consistent with a small district's outturn report; none is a gap worth raising in a first-contact email.
facts.note: The paper is unusually clean for a small district — every arithmetic identity that can be checked ties to the pound except the AIS Total rate (5.88% by our arithmetic vs 6.02% printed; 14bp presentational quirk). Table 8 gives per-line detail down to £0.01 on the residual bank balances — meticulous. The absence of the OLTL total is the only material gap on our side of the reading.

summary.text:
Fifteen-page Capital and Investment Strategy Outturn 2025/26 to Governance Scrutiny Group on 18 June 2026, from Peter Linfield, Director – Finance and Corporate Services (0115 914 8439, plinfield@rushcliffe.gov.uk). Read in full from local PDF. The paper is unusually clean — every arithmetic identity that can be checked ties to the pound except the AIS Total rate (a 14bp presentational quirk).

Rushcliffe is a debt-free small district. The loan-book reconciliation ties zero on zero: price_book.py returns 'no borrower matching Rushcliffe' and the paper at para 4.14 states 'the Council had no recourse to borrow externally during 2025/26 these indicators are not applicable'. The Authorised Limit of £20m and Operational Boundary of £15m were both precautionary and neither was approached. The balance sheet identity can only be checked partially — CFR £8.417m less external £0 leaves £8.417m to be accounted for between OLTL and internal borrowing, but the paper does not print the total lease-liability balance (only the +£66k in-year movement). The NHB Reserve balance of £8.383m sits very close to the CFR and the paper describes it as funding 'internal borrowing for Capital projects (MRP)' — consistent with the reserve essentially underwriting the whole internal position. CFR movement (10,010 + 66 - 1,659 = 8,417) and MRP arithmetic (£1,648k planned + £11k IFRS 16 offset = £1,659k) both tie.

What is distinctive is the investment side. £72.6m invested at 31.3.26 — a substantial net investor. The outturn rate of return was 4.33%, 27bp above the 4.06% budget and 32bp above SONIA (4.01%), producing a net return of £2,051,880 vs £1,434,900 budgeted = +£616,980 favourable. The ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream came in NEGATIVE at (1.33%) because investment income exceeded the £1.659m MRP charge — a distinctive prudential-indicator marker of the debt-free-plus-cash-rich shape.

The strongest single hook in the paper is at Table 8. Rushcliffe's five LA fixed-term deposits are all £5.000m: Cheshire East 4.30% (364d), Blackpool 4.25% (181d), Leeds 4.25% (212d), Lancashire 4.25% (364d) — and then Havant at 5.60% for 30 days (matured 17/04/2026). That is ~160bp over SONIA and 185bp over Base Rate for 30-day money. We hold Havant's own Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 in the library (E07000090): Havant runs a very small external book (£2.7m PWLB, matures 2042) against a £22m CFR — 88% internally funded. A 30-day LA-to-LA bridge at 5.60% fits the profile of an internally-funded district needing a short cash top-up without drawing PWLB. Rushcliffe caught the receive side of that trade — a rate observation the platform is uniquely positioned to make because it reads borrower papers across the sector.

Pooled funds carry a £749,173 cumulative unrealised deficit on £15m invested, but the fair value moved £322k in the council's favour during 2025/26 and Rushcliffe holds a £1.310m mitigation reserve alongside the statutory override to April 2029 — defensively provisioned. The fixed/variable split at 43%/57% sits BELOW the 50% fixed limit despite para 4.18 carving out flexibility to lock in higher rates during the falling cycle — the council did not exercise that flexibility. Not a criticism — the £5m 364-day LA deposits ARE the fixed side — but a notable pattern.

Draft written and machine-checked against the paper text. Contact address (plinfield@rushcliffe.gov.uk) is published on the contact block page 14. Peter's title is 'Director – Finance and Corporate Services' — on constitutional convention that role would typically hold the S151 title but the paper does not state this explicitly, so address in the email is to Peter as Director, not as S151. Send-by set for early autumn 2026 to reach him before the next quarterly treasury update to GSG (date not published; para 4.39 states 'A quarterly update will be presented to this group during 2026/27').

officer.body:
Hi Peter,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Capital and Investment Strategy Outturn you took to Governance Scrutiny Group on 18 June, ahead of the quarterly update that paragraph 4.39 flags for later in 2026/27. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your paper is unusually clean — every arithmetic identity we could check ties to the pound — and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

Two cross-checks first, which is where we start on any paper. Our loan file returns no PWLB entries for Rushcliffe, and your paragraph 4.14 agrees exactly — no recourse to external borrowing during 2025/26 and both the Authorised Limit (£20m) and the Operational Boundary (£15m) held as precautionary. Zero on zero is the strongest form the loan-book cross-check can take. The CFR movement in your Table 3 also ties to the pound (opening £10.010m plus the £66k IFRS 16 adjustment less the £1.659m MRP equals your closing £8.417m), and inside the £1.659m the split you note at paragraph 4.11 works out precisely (£1.648m planned plus £11k for the IFRS 16 offset). Rare on both.

What first caught our eye, though, is on Table 8. Your five local-authority fixed-term deposits are each £5.000m — four of them at 4.25% or 4.30% for tenors between 181 and 364 days, and then Havant at 5.60% for 30 days, matured 17 April. Your paragraph 4.21 gives SONIA for 2025-26 at 4.01% and your paragraph 4.20 has Bank Rate at 3.75% since December, so 5.60% for 30-day money is around 160 basis points over SONIA and 185 over Base Rate for the tenor. That is a stand-out rate. We happen to hold Havant's own 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy, and the shape of it is consistent with a small internally-funded council needing a very short cash top-up rather than drawing PWLB — the position across the wider sector's small districts, which we read from the borrower side, is that these short LA-to-LA bridges quietly clear at premium rates. Nothing follows from us as advice; the observation is simply that Rushcliffe caught the receive side of a trade we can characterise from both sides of the market, which is an unusual vantage.

While we're on the LA side of the book, the shape more broadly is worth noting. £25m across five councils at £5m each is a very clean concentration cap — of the councils we've read this year, that discipline is at the higher end. And the two of your five counterparties whose own recent treasury papers we've read (we'll not name which two here — Rushcliffe knows its own counterparties and specifying tips into implying we pass information between authorities, which we don't) both fit the borrower-side profile you'd expect. If it's useful, our /pwlb-activity page carries the monthly PWLB volumes by council and tenor, which is the closest external reference for what those five counterparties are doing on the borrowing side of their books when your deposits come back for redeployment.

Your ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream at Table 4 is the second thing worth naming. The actual came in negative at minus 1.33% against a positive 1.67% budget, because your investment income exceeded the £1.659m MRP charge — you flag this plainly at paragraph 4.16. A negative financing-costs ratio is a distinctive prudential-indicator marker of the debt-free-plus-cash-rich shape. On the £617k investment income beat (£2.051m actual against £1.435m budget on our arithmetic, ties to the pound), some of it is the 27bp your outturn 4.33% ran over budget 4.06%, on a £72.6m book — a genuine performance outcome. And some of it is the wider environment: your deposits placed at 4.25-5.60% were placed when the market was pricing higher, and as the sub-12-month ladder rolls through 2026 those rates will re-set into whatever the money-market curve gives at each redemption date.

One standing observation. The liability benchmark work at our /loan-analysis page is interactive and live, which matters given CIPFA has updates to the Prudential and Treasury Codes coming. Your Chart 1 already prints the benchmark and it sits well below zero throughout the forecast — the Council remains a substantial net investor — but the platform view is useful for understanding how peers' benchmarks compare and where they cross, particularly for districts running LGR-driven capital pipeline changes.
